share.headline: A flyer-app recommendation became a diss track and a counter-group.
share.text:
Someone wanted a flyer app with no AI. I somehow ended up with a diss track and a group called Artists Against Artists Against Generative AI.

A very normal response to a software recommendation. Open the backstory and meet the resistance to the resistance.
share.description: One request for flyer software without AI became a dubstep diss and a deliberately ridiculous counter-group. Open the origin story.
share.title: A flyer-app recommendation became a diss track and a counter-group. — Anti Generative AI Diss

share.headline: Before Armando became a question, he was a laugh that got out of hand.
share.text: I noticed my laugh in a reaction recording, isolated it, and kept following it until Armando had his own song. This is the earlier mix, before the final question gave the joke its payoff. Open it and meet the laugh that started the trouble.
share.description: A laugh pulled from a reaction recording became Armando. This earlier mix preserves a step on the way to the chosen version.
share.title: Before Armando became a question, he was a laugh that got out of hand. — Armando — Earlier Mix

share.headline: One burned car. One spectacularly bad fictional explanation.
share.text:
A burned car in Red Deer needed an explanation. I supplied a spectacularly bad fictional one.

It involves a wife, her sister, and a man with absolutely no survival instincts. Open Ashes in Eastwood for the consequences. Bring marshmallows.
share.description: A real burned car sparked a deliberately trashy fictional disaster involving a wife, her sister, and a terrible decision. Open Ashes in Eastwood.
share.title: One burned car. One spectacularly bad fictional explanation. — Ashes in Eastwood

share.headline: If new tools don’t count, Gary’s loud rock remains undefeated.
share.text: Someone has rejected every new instrument and is now defending a rock. Back to Sticks turns AI-music gatekeeping into a caveman field study—with an actual guide to the listening, editing and judgment behind the joke. Open the field guide. Bring your emergency stick.
share.description: The rocks have entered the chat. A caveman roast doubles as a guide to the decisions behind AI-assisted music.
share.title: If new tools don’t count, Gary’s loud rock remains undefeated. — Back to Sticks (Soothing Mix)

rows.title: Broke My Mug Not My Song
rows.label: Lo-fi Warehouse Techno Mix

share.headline: I got through an Alberta winter. Then my favourite mug broke.
share.text: The mug had followed me through car-sales jobs. After my first Alberta winter outside, it fell in the van around the time the person who gave it to me left my life. Open Broke My Mug Not My Song for the small object that carried more than coffee.
share.description: A favourite mug, several jobs, a winter outside, and the person who gave it to me. Read what was lost when it broke.
share.title: I got through an Alberta winter. Then my favourite mug broke. — Broke My Mug Not My Song

share.headline: No confession. No discussion. The suspect is three aisles over.
share.text:
A grocery aisle. A mysterious change in atmosphere. A suspect who has already moved on to buying flour.

Canadian politeness has apparently extended to refusing to discuss the evidence.

Open Canadian Crop Dusting for the joke, the lyrics, and the beat's unlikely backstory.
share.description: Grocery-aisle comments became a crop-dusting mystery. Read the joke and follow the beat back through a homemade DAW and a sample of Satan's Loan.
share.title: No confession. No discussion. The suspect is three aisles over. — Canadian Crop Dusting

share.headline: Who buys a ticket when we sit and fix it?
share.text:
A parent. An adult child. A crowd cheering on each side.

In this imagined movie scene, the argument changes when they start talking to their audiences instead of each other.

Read Cheap to Inform—and the question about why we keep watching the fight.
share.description: An imagined movie scene about a family argument and the audiences around it. Read Cheap to Inform: fictional perspectives, not the writer's family history.
share.title: Who buys a ticket when we sit and fix it? — Cheap to Inform

share.headline: A cloud gives itself away. We call it bad weather.
share.text:
A cloud spends its whole life giving itself away. Then we call it bad weather.

A rainy stretch in Red Deer became Cloudlife—a little tale about carrying too much, letting go, and changing form. Open it and follow the water.
share.description: A rainy stretch in Red Deer became a cloud’s tale of giving, letting go, and returning in another form. Follow Cloudlife through the sky.
share.title: A cloud gives itself away. We call it bad weather. — Cloudlife · The Life of a Cloud

share.headline: Two wheelbarrows of concrete. Naturally, a 5:44 ballad.
share.text:
Two wheelbarrows of concrete. One community post. Naturally, I made a 5:44 ballad.

The trees deserved care. The situation apparently also required a chorus. Open the story, read the lyrics, and consider the terrifying possibility of wheelbarrow number three.
share.description: Two small wheelbarrows at Big Dipper Park inspired one very dramatic musical response. Read the story and lyrics of Concrete Under Evergreens.
share.title: Two wheelbarrows of concrete. Naturally, a 5:44 ballad. — Concrete Under Evergreens

share.headline: Same two jokes. One beat on a loop. That can be a whole evening.
share.text: A couple of friends, late-night calls, and messy ideas turning into sound. Couple Friends Couple Calls finds its moment in the small stuff: showing up, laughing again, pressing record. Open the page and drop into that room for a while.
share.description: Late-night calls, familiar jokes and a beat on a loop. A small scene about making something with the people who show up.
share.title: Same two jokes. One beat on a loop. That can be a whole evening. — Couple Friends Couple Calls

rows.title: Cut From the Same Fabric — Instrumental
rows.label: instrumental

share.headline: The words picked sides. What happens when you take them away?
share.text: One song split into two arguments: bitterness, and the part worth keeping. This is the space between them—the related musical fabric with the words removed. Open the instrumental from Cut From the Same Fabric and hear what remains when neither side is talking.
share.description: Between Find Your People and HELL HAS PEOPLE TOO, the instrumental leaves the words out of the argument.
share.title: The words picked sides. What happens when you take them away? — Cut From the Same Fabric — Instrumental

rows.title: Did Armando Die After You Held His Beer?
rows.label: chosen version

share.headline: Everybody says “hold my beer.” Who checks on Armando afterward?
share.text: You held the beer. Armando made a decision. Now there are follow-up questions. A laugh from a reaction recording became this increasingly unreasonable joke. Open the chosen version and decide whether “hold my beer” needed a follow-up form.
share.description: A reaction, a laugh, a sample—and the question after “hold my beer.” Meet the chosen Armando version.
share.title: Everybody says “hold my beer.” Who checks on Armando afterward? — Did Armando Die After You Held His Beer?

share.headline: “You don't like me? I don't like me.”
share.text:
“You don't like me? I don't like me.”

Then the feeling gets handed to somebody else in a comment or a joke that cuts too deep.

Read Everybody Else Less, a fictional narrator's spiral from self-dislike into spite—and the hurt underneath it.
share.description: A fictional narrator turns self-dislike outward. Read Everybody Else Less for the hurt under the jokes, the comments, and the spite.
share.title: “You don't like me? I don't like me.” — Everybody Else Less

share.headline: What if you kept the boundary and left the bitterness behind?
share.text: One song was trying to be two: resentment on one side, something worth keeping on the other. Find Your People is the part I kept—finding people who don’t need you smaller. Open this side of Cut From the Same Fabric and start with what’s worth carrying forward.
share.description: The part worth keeping after one song split in two: boundaries, growth, and people who do not need you smaller.
share.title: What if you kept the boundary and left the bitterness behind? — Find Your People

share.headline: What if the mask has started to feel like your face?
share.text:
How do you let someone see you when the mask has started to feel like your face?

Fractured Face follows that fear: hiding the hurt, wanting love, and not knowing how to take the mask off. Open the May 2026 remaster.
share.description: Hiding the hurt can also hide the person who wants to be loved. Step into the fear behind Fractured Face, preserved here in its May 2026 remaster.
share.title: What if the mask has started to feel like your face? — Fractured Face

share.headline: Was there a shortcut you missed—or a long road you’re still making sense of?
share.text: “You didn’t need acid” is the line at the centre of Friction the What. The writing looks back at cold van nights, loss and contradiction, asking what actually changed its narrator. Open the page and follow that question through the song.
share.description: Cold van nights, loss, contradiction—and the question of whether a missed shortcut would really have changed anything.
share.title: Was there a shortcut you missed—or a long road you’re still making sense of? — Friction the What

share.headline: One mouth-made beat. One list of the world’s problems. Bad combination.
share.text: I recorded myself going “unce, unce, unce,” then recorded a humorous rush through the world’s problems. Those two clips became Funhouse Meltdown. Open the page to see where my voice ends and Suno’s production begins—and how the overload became the point.
share.description: Two recordings of my voice—one beat, one overloaded list—became Funhouse Meltdown. Read how the source clips shaped the production.
share.title: One mouth-made beat. One list of the world’s problems. Bad combination. — Funhouse Meltdown

share.headline: Some mornings, being here is already the hard part.
share.text:
Some mornings, being here is already the hard part.

Hard-Earned Light starts with the nights that make you question your worth and reaches for a reason to keep building. Open it when you want that struggle given a voice.
share.description: The nights that make you question your worth, and the effort of reaching another morning. Open Hard-Earned Light for words about keeping going.
share.title: Some mornings, being here is already the hard part. — Hard-Earned Light

share.text:
Would you choose love if the hurt came in the same package?

Heartbreak, Heartbreak, You Water Me says yes, even with the loss still fresh. Open the 2026 remix of a piano-and-voice rehearsal made in Nova Scotia before the move west.
share.description: A heartbreak song that still chooses love. Open the 2026 remix of a Nova Scotia piano-and-voice rehearsal from before the move to Alberta.
share.title: Would you choose love if the hurt came in the same package? — Heartbreak, Heartbreak, You Water Me

share.headline: Some people call it support. Why does it come with a scoreboard?
share.text: The smiles when you fall. The silence when you grow. HELL HAS PEOPLE TOO takes the jealousy and resentment cut out of another song and gives them somewhere to speak. Open the darker side of Cut From the Same Fabric and hear what got left behind.
share.description: Jealousy, comparison and support that keeps score. This is the bitter cut from a song that was trying to say two different things.
share.title: Some people call it support. Why does it come with a scoreboard? — HELL HAS PEOPLE TOO

share.headline: What if the person you were trying to become never arrives?
share.text:
Everyone says keep going. Nobody tells you what to do when you no longer believe in the person you were trying to become.

Keep Moving sits inside that question—and keeps going anyway. Open it if that sounds familiar.
share.description: The plan keeps changing. The promised future self feels further away. Keep Moving gives that uncertainty a voice without pretending the route is clear.
share.title: What if the person you were trying to become never arrives? — Keep Moving · v2

Read the original poem and follow it into the music video.
